level1.text: A cyclist rides uniformly at $5.5\,\text{m/s}$. How far does the cyclist travel in $20\,\text{s}$?
A runner covers $360\,\text{m}$ in $45\,\text{s}$ at a steady pace. What is the runner's speed?

The graph shows the position of a walker as a function of time. The walker keeps moving uniformly in the same direction also beyond the graph. How many seconds pass from the start until the walker has travelled $150\,\text{m}$?
An object moves uniformly from its starting point and travels $18\,\text{m}$ in $4.0\,\text{s}$. How far does it travel in $10\,\text{s}$?

The position of a uniformly moving trolley, measured from the starting point, is $7.0\,\text{m}$ at $2.0\,\text{s}$ and $21\,\text{m}$ at $6.0\,\text{s}$. Calculate the speed of the trolley using the change in position and the time interval.
The position $s$ of a walker has been measured as a function of time $t$, and the measurement points lie on a straight line. What does the slope $\Delta s : \Delta t$ of the line tell?

choices.feedback: Correct: the slope is the change in position divided by the time interval, and in uniform motion it is the speed $v$. Its unit is m/s.
The initial position $s_0$ is where the line crosses the $s$-axis, that is, the position at time $t = 0$, not the slope. The slope tells how steeply the position changes.

choices.text: The total distance the walker travelled.
choices.feedback: The total distance is the difference $\Delta s$ between the position at the end of the line and the initial position. The slope is obtained when this is further divided by the time interval $\Delta t$.

choices.text: The quotient $s : t$ of position $s$ and time $t$ at some single point.
choices.feedback: The quotient $s : t$ is the speed only if the line passes through the origin. If $s_0 \neq 0$, the speed is the change in position per time, $\Delta s : \Delta t$.

level1.text: The $(t, v)$ graph of a uniformly moving trolley is a horizontal line at $v = 0.80\,\text{m/s}$ during the interval $0\text{–}12\,\text{s}$. The area of the rectangle between the line and the $t$-axis corresponds to the distance travelled. How far does the trolley travel during this time?
A cyclist travels uniformly $2.4\,\text{km}$ in $16\,\text{min}$. What is the cyclist's speed? Give the answer in m/s.

level2.text: A car drives at a constant speed of $54\,\text{km/h}$. How far does it travel in $14\,\text{s}$? Give the answer in metres.
A bus drives uniformly at $36\,\text{km/h}$. How many seconds does a distance of $4.5\,\text{km}$ take?

A hiker is at a point $1.5\,\text{km}$ from a cabin. The hiker walks along a straight path away from the cabin, uniformly at $1.5\,\text{m/s}$. How far from the cabin is the hiker after $10\,\text{min}$? Give the answer in kilometres.

After a flash of lightning, the rumble of thunder is heard $5.0\,\text{s}$ later. Sound travels in air uniformly at $343\,\text{m/s}$, and the travel time of light is so small that it is ignored. How far away did the lightning strike? Give the answer in kilometres.

The motion of a walker was filmed, and the position $s$ of the walker from the starting mark was measured by video analysis as a function of time $t$. The walker moves uniformly, and the points deviate from a straight line because of measurement uncertainty.

Draw a graph of the points and fit a straight line to them. Determine the speed of the walker from the slope of the line and use it to predict the position of the walker at time $12\,\text{s}$. How many metres from the starting mark is the walker then? Justify why the prediction is a model value and not a measurement.

data.caption: Position of the walker as a function of time

level2.text: A trolley moves uniformly on a track. It is initially at $s_0 = 8.0\,\text{m}$, and at time $2.0\,\text{s}$ it is at $11\,\text{m}$. A student reasons: “When the time triples to $6.0\,\text{s}$, the position triples, so the trolley is then at $33\,\text{m}$.” Find the student's error and calculate the correct position of the trolley at time $6.0\,\text{s}$.

A toy car drives uniformly at about $0.80\,\text{m/s}$. The travel time of the car is measured by hand, and the uncertainty of the timing is about $0.2\,\text{s}$ regardless of the length of the time measured.

You are planning a measurement of the speed in which the relative uncertainty of the time must be at most $2.0\,\%$. Assume that the distance is measured so accurately that its uncertainty does not affect the result.

What is the minimum distance the car must travel during the measurement? Explain why a long distance improves the measurement.

A walker first stands still for $4.0\,\text{s}$ at a point $6.0\,\text{m}$ from the starting point. Then she walks steadily at a speed of $1.0\,\text{m/s}$ straight back towards the starting point until she is there. The position $s$ is measured from the starting point.

Which of the graphs shows the position $s$ of the walker as a function of time $t$?

choices.feedback: In this graph the position increases to $12\,\text{m}$, so the walker would move away from the starting point. When the walker returns towards the starting point, the position $s$ decreases, so the line must go down and not up.

This is a $(t, v)$ graph: the vertical axis shows the speed $v$, not the position $s$. In it, standing still is $v = 0$ and steady walking is a horizontal line, but in a position graph a horizontal line means staying in place. You cannot see from this graph where the walker is, nor that she is at $6.0\,\text{m}$ at the start. Even as a velocity graph B would not be right: the position decreases on the way back, so the velocity $v = \Delta s : \Delta t = -1.0\,\text{m/s}$ is negative.

Correct: the position stays at $6.0\,\text{m}$ at first, so the line is horizontal. Then the position decreases steadily by $6.0\,\text{m}$ in $6.0\,\text{s}$, so the line goes down and the walker is at the starting point at the time $10\,\text{s}$.

The vertical axis of this graph shows the distance walked $\Delta s$, not the position $s$: the distance is zero while standing and then grows to $6.0\,\text{m}$. The position tells where the walker is, so it starts from $6.0\,\text{m}$ and not from zero, and it decreases on the way back.

level3.text:
The Voyager 2 probe crossed the heliopause on 5 November 2018 at a distance of $119.0\,\text{AU}$ from the Sun (Burlaga et al. 2019), and its speed relative to the Sun was then $15.341\,\text{km/s}$ (NASA/JPL). Assume the speed is constant.

How many days after the heliopause crossing is the probe, according to the model, $150\,\text{AU}$ from the Sun? Use the values $1\,\text{AU} = 149\,597\,870.7\,\text{km}$ and $1\,\text{day} = 86\,400\,\text{s}$. The result is a model value.

Assume that Voyager 2 is at a distance of $150\,\text{AU}$ from the Earth. A radio signal travels in vacuum uniformly at $299\,792\,458\,\text{m/s}$.

How many hours pass from the moment a command leaves the Earth to the moment the reply of the probe reaches the Earth? The motion of the probe and its processing time for the reply are ignored. Use the value $1\,\text{AU} = 149\,597\,870.7\,\text{km}$. Justify why the motion can be ignored.

Two friends set off from the school door along the same straight street in the same direction. The first walks uniformly at $1.5\,\text{m/s}$. The second leaves the door $40\,\text{s}$ later on a bicycle and rides uniformly at $4.5\,\text{m/s}$. How far from the door does the cyclist catch up with the walker?

The position $s$ of a cyclist from the start of the track was measured by video analysis as a function of time $t$. Draw a graph of the points.

The cyclist's speed changes partway, so the motion cannot be modelled with a single straight line. Find in the table the moment when the speed changes, and model the motion as two uniform parts.

Use the model to calculate the cyclist's average speed in the interval $5.0\text{–}35\,\text{s}$, where the average speed is the change in position divided by the length of the interval. The moment $35\,\text{s}$ is not in the table. Why is the average speed not the mean of the speeds of the parts?

data.caption: Position of the cyclist as a function of time

level3.text:
A fast bullet is filmed with a camera that takes a picture every $0.010\,\text{s}$. The position $s$ of the bullet from the starting point, measured from the pictures, is in the table. The speed of the bullet is constant during this time. Calculate the speed of the bullet.

A $(t, s)$ graph is drawn in which $1.0\,\text{s}$ on the horizontal axis is $10\,\text{cm}$ and $1.0\,\text{m}$ on the vertical axis is $1.0\,\text{cm}$.

How many centimetres does the line rise during one imaging interval, and how long is the imaging interval on the horizontal axis? Use these to justify why the line looks almost vertical but cannot be exactly vertical.

data.caption: Position of the bullet as a function of time
